# Opening

## The cross-reference twin

The first index marks a term the second index's cross-reference points at,
two chapters further on. A target is resolved against the marks of its own
index, so that one dangles; an accumulator merged across both indexes would
resolve it against this mark and say nothing at all.
[Solvent]{.index}.

A cross-reference of the first index's own, whose target the first index does
mark: it resolves, and must draw no report.
[Reagent]{.index see="Solvent"}.

## The sort-key twin

The same printed path, keyed once in each index. A sort key written in one
index says nothing about where the same printed text files in the other, so
this key is no rival of the second index's two.
[Rival]{.index sort="Mmm"}.

The second index's own first key for that path, which is the one that wins:
[Rival]{.index index="second" sort="Aaa"}.

## The range twin

A range opened in the first index and closed in the second, in the next
chapter. The two never face each other, because a range pairs inside one
index, so the book names neither of them; a merged pairing map would name
both as a pair split across chapters.
[Crossed]{.index range="open"}.

The second index's own opening, whose closing is in the next chapter and in
that same index: [Bridge]{.index index="second" range="open"}.
